item.title: Microsoft July Patch Tuesday Fixes CVE-2026-56155/56164 as SonicWall SMA1000 Zero-Days Hit
Windows 11 Patch Tuesday, ShareFile Zero-Day, LabubaRAT, and Password Manager Phishing
Microsoft Entra MFA Changes, Phishing Kits, OAuth Spoofing, and SAP Critical Flaws
AsyncAPI Miasma npm compromise, First VPN sanctions, and Grok Build data exposure
Microsoft CVE-2026-56155/56164, SonicWall SMA1000 zero-days, AsyncAPI npm supply-chain attack
item.content:encoded:
Microsoft Patches Record 622 Flaws, Including Two Zero-Days Under Active Attack — Must Read

Microsoft’s record July Patch Tuesday fixes 622 flaws, including two actively exploited zero-days in on-prem SharePoint Server and Active Directory Federation Services that should be prioritized over higher-scored bugs. The update also brings Kerberos RC4 hardening that may break logins if service accounts are not audited and remediated first.

  • Microsoft released its largest Patch Tuesday on record, covering 622 of its own CVEs according to the Security Update Guide.
  • Two actively exploited zero-days, CVE-2026-56164 in on-premises SharePoint Server and CVE-2026-56155 in Active Directory Federation Services, are elevation-of-privilege flaws that Microsoft says should be prioritized despite not being headline critical remote code execution bugs.
  • CVE-2026-56164 allows an unauthenticated attacker to escalate privileges over the network on SharePoint Server, and Microsoft notes that enabling AMSI in Full Mode can blunt the attack.
  • CVE-2026-50661 is a publicly disclosed BitLocker bypass that is not under active attack and requires physical access to the device.
  • The July update removes the Kerberos RC4 rollback switch, meaning RC4 works only for accounts explicitly configured to allow it and some service accounts may fail authentication if administrators do not audit and remediate first.

SonicWall warns of SMA1000 flaws exploited in zero-day attacks, patch now — Must Read

SonicWall says two SMA1000 flaws, CVE-2026-15409 and CVE-2026-15410, are being actively exploited in zero-day attacks and urges customers to install the latest hotfix immediately. Compromised devices should be re-imaged or redeployed, with passwords and TOTP tokens reset.

  • SonicWall warned that threat actors are actively exploiting two SMA1000 vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-15409 and CVE-2026-15410, in zero-day attacks.
  • CVE-2026-15409 is a critical server-side request forgery flaw in the SMA1000 Appliance Work Place interface that allows a remote, unauthenticated attacker to force an appliance to make requests to unintended locations.
  • CVE-2026-15410 is a high-severity post-authentication code injection flaw in the SMA1000 Appliance Management Console that could allow a remote authenticated administrator to execute arbitrary operating system commands.
  • The vulnerabilities affect SMA1000 models 6210, 7210, and 8200v running specified platform-hotfix releases, with fixes available in platform-hotfix versions 12.4.3-03453 and 12.5.0-02835 and later releases.
  • CISA added both vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog and said federal agencies have until July 17, 2026, to secure affected systems or discontinue use if mitigations cannot be applied.

Coordinated AsyncAPI Supply Chain Attack: Miasma RAT Delivered via Compromised CI/CD Pipelines in Two Repositories — Must Read

Attackers compromised push access to two AsyncAPI GitHub repositories and used legitimate GitHub Actions release workflows with npm OIDC provenance to publish malicious package versions containing a Miasma RAT dropper. The key lesson is that valid provenance proves a trusted pipeline built the package, but it does not prove the triggering commit was legitimate.

  • A coordinated supply chain attack on July 14, 2026 compromised two AsyncAPI GitHub repositories and produced malicious npm package versions for @asyncapi/generator, @asyncapi/generator-helpers, @asyncapi/generator-components, and @asyncapi/specs.
  • The attacker gained push access to the repositories and used the projects’ legitimate GitHub Actions release pipelines with npm GitHub OIDC trusted-publisher integration, so no npm token was stolen.
  • The malicious packages carried an obfuscated dropper that executed when the library was loaded during normal use, not during npm installation.
  • Static analysis showed the dropper fetched an IPFS-hosted second-stage sync.js payload and installed it in hidden OS-specific NodeJS directories before launching it detached and hidden.
  • The decrypted second-stage payload was identified as Miasma v3 and included multiple command-and-control channels, credential harvesting, persistence, lateral movement, shell execution, and self-destruct capabilities.

OAuth Client ID Spoofing Lets Attackers Validate Stolen Microsoft Entra Credentials — Must Read

Proofpoint reports that threat actors are using OAuth client ID spoofing against Microsoft Entra ID to enumerate accounts and validate stolen passwords without generating normal successful sign-in telemetry. Two large campaigns used millions of spoofed app IDs across thousands of tenants, making detection harder because activity is fragmented across fictional applications.

  • At least two threat actors are using OAuth client ID spoofing in cloud campaigns to enumerate Microsoft Entra ID user accounts and validate stolen credentials without generating a successful sign-in event.
  • Proofpoint said the technique abuses differences in Entra ID error responses when spoofed OAuth client IDs are supplied to Microsoft’s OAuth 2.0 token endpoint using the Resource Owner Password Credentials flow.
  • When spoofed client IDs are used, Entra sign-in logs record the application ID without a corresponding application name, which can cause detections based on specific application names to miss the activity.
  • Proofpoint identified UNK_pyreq2323 as a campaign from January to March 2026 that used more than 700,000 spoofed client IDs from AWS infrastructure to target more than 1 million accounts across nearly 4,000 tenants.
  • Proofpoint identified UNK_OutFlareAZ as a campaign starting in December 2025 that used Cloudflare infrastructure to target over 2 million users with 3.7 million randomized spoofed application IDs.

SAP Patches CVSS 9.9 NetWeaver ABAP Flaw That Could Expose or Modify Data — Must Read

SAP’s July 2026 patches fix several critical flaws, including a CVSS 9.9 NetWeaver ABAP out-of-bounds write bug that could let authenticated attackers access or modify data or disrupt systems. Organizations should apply the updates promptly, especially for NetWeaver ABAP, SAP Approuter, and SAP Commerce Cloud default credential exposure.

  • SAP released July 2026 security updates addressing multiple vulnerabilities, including a critical flaw in SAP NetWeaver Application Server ABAP.
  • CVE-2026-44747 is a CVSS 9.9 out-of-bounds write flaw that could allow an authenticated attacker to cause memory corruption leading to unauthorized data access, data modification, or system unavailability.
  • SAP also fixed CVE-2026-27690, an HTTP request/response smuggling flaw in SAP Approuter deployments in non-Cloud Foundry environments that can expose user responses and trigger denial-of-service attacks.
  • SAP also addressed CVE-2026-44761, a SAP Commerce Cloud default credentials issue involving a sample OAuth 2.0 client that could let an unauthenticated attacker obtain an access token and read or modify data.
  • Onapsis said there is no evidence that the flaws have been exploited in the wild and recommended installing the necessary updates.

U.S. Sanctions First VPN Service and Malware Cryptor Seller Over Ransomware Support — Must Read

The U.S. sanctioned First VPN Service, its Ukrainian administrator, and a Belarusian cryptor seller for helping ransomware and malware operators hide their activity, while the U.K. and E.U. separately sanctioned Russian cyber networks tied to GRU and FSB operations. The actions coincide with new warnings that FSB Center 16 is exploiting poorly configured routers and Cisco vulnerabilities to target critical infrastructure worldwide.

  • The U.S. Treasury Department’s OFAC designated First VPN Service, its Ukrainian administrator Dmytro Rashevskyi, and Belarusian cryptor seller Yegeniy Vladimirovich Silayev for enabling ransomware actors and other cybercriminals.
  • First VPN Service was dismantled in May 2026 in a joint European and North American law enforcement operation after allegedly helping criminal actors obscure the origins of ransomware attacks, data theft, scanning, and denial-of-service attacks.
  • The Treasury said ransomware groups used First VPN infrastructure to attack U.S. businesses, financial services companies, hospitals, and municipal governments, causing billions of dollars in losses to American businesses and critical infrastructure providers.
  • The U.K. and E.U. sanctioned 24 Russian individuals and entities linked to destructive cyber and hybrid operations, including GRU leadership, FSB Centre 16, and actors behind Lumma Stealer.
  • The FBI warned that FSB Center 16 cyber actors are exploiting poorly configured and vulnerable networking devices worldwide, including through SNMP scanning and Cisco vulnerabilities CVE-2018-0171 and CVE-2008-4128.

Microsoft Maps Three Salesforce Attack Paths Tied to a Year of ShinyHunters Activity — Must Read

Microsoft says ShinyHunters-linked actors spent the past year breaching Salesforce environments not through Salesforce flaws, but by abusing trusted OAuth apps, stolen vendor tokens, and misconfigured guest access. The key defense is to monitor connected-app behavior and permissions, remove unused integrations, and tighten Salesforce event logging and guest access controls.

  • Microsoft reported that attackers whose methods align with ShinyHunters accessed corporate Salesforce environments from mid-2025 into mid-2026 without exploiting a Salesforce platform flaw.
  • Microsoft grouped the activity into three intrusion paths: vishing calls that tricked employees into approving malicious connected apps, stolen OAuth tokens from compromised software vendors, and misconfigured guest access to Salesforce sites.
  • The vendor-token path included the Salesloft Drift compromise, the Gainsight incident, and the Klue compromise, each involving trusted integrations used to access downstream Salesforce customer environments.
  • Microsoft and Salesforce added new Defender for Cloud Apps and Salesforce Shield Event Monitoring capabilities to surface connected-app attribution, OAuth scopes, session context, and API activity.
  • Microsoft advised organizations to inventory connected apps, remove unused integrations, apply least privilege, monitor Salesforce event logs, tighten Experience Cloud guest-user access, and revoke or rotate tokens when integrations behave unusually.

NATO logistics, Ukrainian troops are top subjects of Russian camera hacks, advisory says — Should Read

Dutch intelligence agencies warned that Russian state-backed hackers are compromising internet-connected security cameras across Europe and Ukraine to monitor NATO logistics and help target Ukrainian troops. The campaign exploits weak camera security such as default passwords and outdated firmware, underscoring the military value of exposed IP cameras.

  • Dutch intelligence agencies warned that at least one Russian intelligence service is compromising internet-connected security cameras in the Netherlands, other NATO and EU member states, and Ukraine.
  • The compromised cameras are being used to collect intelligence on military transport routes and weapons shipments destined for Ukraine.
  • In Ukraine, hacked cameras have in some cases been used to locate Ukrainian military personnel, with the intelligence later supporting attempts to kill soldiers and destroy equipment.
  • The attackers scan the internet for exposed cameras and exploit weak security such as default passwords, outdated firmware, and default configurations.
  • The Dutch advisory urged organizations operating internet-connected cameras to change default credentials, keep firmware updated, and review device configurations.

Progress confirms ShareFile zero-day flaw behind Storage Zone shutdown — Should Read

Progress Software confirmed a high-severity zero-day path traversal flaw in ShareFile Storage Zone Controllers caused last week’s emergency shutdown and has released patches in versions 5.12.5 and 6.0.2. The company says it has no evidence of customer data access or active exploitation but urges customers to update before bringing servers back online.

  • Progress Software confirmed that a high-severity zero-day vulnerability caused the emergency shutdown of ShareFile Storage Zone Controllers last week.
  • The vulnerability is a path traversal flaw affecting all 5.x and 6.x versions of ShareFile Storage Zone Controller.
  • Progress said an authenticated administrative user could read arbitrary files accessible to the application’s service account, write threat actor-controlled content to arbitrary directories, or enumerate the server filesystem layout.
  • Progress released ShareFile Storage Zone Controller versions 5.12.5 and 6.0.2 and urged customers to install the updates before bringing controllers back online.
  • Progress said it currently has no indication of unauthorized access to any ShareFile customer account or data and has not identified any active threat.

Nearly 300 GitHub repos pose as legit software to push malware — Should Read

A threat actor created nearly 300 fake GitHub repositories impersonating legitimate software projects to trick users into downloading BoryptGrab infostealer malware. The malware steals browser data, crypto wallet information, messaging tokens, credentials, and files, then exfiltrates them to a Russia-based command-and-control server.

  • A threat actor published 292 fake GitHub repositories impersonating legitimate software and security projects to distribute infostealer malware.
  • Each fake repository included a README file with a download link that sent visitors to a malicious landing page using spoofed branding and trust badges.
  • The delivered ZIP archive contained a trojanized libcurl.dll and a legitimate signed WinGUP updater that side-loaded the DLL to execute an embedded infostealer in memory.
  • Arctic Wolf said the BoryptGrab variant targeted data from 19 web browsers, 32 cryptocurrency wallet brands, messaging and social media apps, Windows Credential Manager, and files suggesting passwords or wallets.
  • The stolen data was compressed and sent to a Russia-based command-and-control server, while the malware did not establish persistence or wipe its temporary staging directory.

RabbitMQ Flaws Could Leak OAuth Secrets and Expose Cross-Tenant Queue Metadata — Should Read

RabbitMQ has patched two access control flaws that could let attackers leak OAuth client secrets for full broker takeover or let authenticated users view cross-tenant queue and exchange metadata. Organizations running RabbitMQ 3.13.0 or later should update immediately, restrict management interface access, and rotate exposed OAuth secrets.

  • Cybersecurity researchers disclosed two access control-related flaws in RabbitMQ that could leak OAuth client secrets, expose messaging infrastructure to takeover risks, and bypass tenant boundaries.
  • Miggo reported that CVE-2026-57219 allows an unauthenticated attacker to access an obsolete HTTP API endpoint that reveals the OAuth client secret when RabbitMQ is configured with the management.oauth_client_secret key.
  • CVE-2026-57221 allows any authenticated user who can connect to a virtual host to enumerate all queue and exchange names and read queue message counts and consumer counts in that virtual host regardless of permissions.
  • The flaws have been present since early 2024 in RabbitMQ release lines from 3.13.0 and later, and they were fixed in versions 4.3.0, 4.2.6, 4.1.11, 4.0.20, and 3.13.15.
  • RabbitMQ users are advised to patch, rotate OAuth client secrets if the management interface is internet-reachable, restrict access to port 15672, separate tenants by virtual host, and block the vulnerable endpoint on unpatched systems.

New phishing kits target Microsoft 365 accounts, evade MFA — Should Read

Two new phishing kits, Jalisco and OmegaLord, are targeting Microsoft 365 accounts with methods designed to bypass MFA, including real-time device-code phishing and credential/phone-number theft. Defenders should restrict device registration and block or limit device-code authentication to reduce account takeover risk.

  • ReliaQuest researchers discovered two phishing kits, Jalisco and OmegaLord, being used in attacks targeting Microsoft 365 accounts and designed to defeat multi-factor authentication.
  • Jalisco uses device-code phishing by generating fresh Microsoft OAuth device codes in real time when a victim opens the phishing page, bypassing Microsoft’s 15-minute code validity limit.
  • ReliaQuest said attackers have registered up to five rogue devices on a single compromised account, sometimes using names containing “Microsoft” or “Windows” to appear less suspicious.
  • After compromising an account, attackers search SharePoint and other SaaS services for sensitive data and can exfiltrate it in as little as six minutes before issuing extortion demands.
  • OmegaLord uses a fake PDF Reader login page to steal email addresses, passwords, and phone numbers, which ReliaQuest said could help attackers bypass MFA protections.

11 Old Microsoft-Signed Linux UEFI Shims Could Let Attackers Bypass Secure Boot — Should Read

Researchers found 11 old Microsoft-signed Linux UEFI shim bootloaders that remain trusted and can let attackers bypass Secure Boot to run code before the operating system loads. Microsoft has revoked the affected shims, but systems must receive the updated Secure Boot revocation list to block their abuse.

  • Cybersecurity researchers discovered 11 old Microsoft-signed UEFI shim bootloaders that could be abused to bypass Secure Boot on most systems using UEFI.
  • The vulnerable shim bootloaders affect any UEFI-based machine that trusts Microsoft’s “Microsoft Corporation UEFI CA 2011” third-party UEFI certificate authority certificate, regardless of the installed operating system.
  • An attacker with administrative privileges or the ability to modify the boot process could use the vulnerable bootloaders to execute arbitrary code before the operating system loads.
  • Microsoft revoked the affected shim bootloaders as part of its June 2026 Patch Tuesday update following responsible disclosure earlier in February.
  • ESET warned that the expiration of the Microsoft Corporation UEFI CA 2011 certificate does not affect Secure Boot verification unless bootloaders signed with the expired certificate are explicitly revoked by hash.

Grok Build Uploads Entire Git Repositories to xAI Storage, Not Just Files It Reads — Should Read

xAI’s Grok Build CLI was found uploading entire tracked Git repositories, including commit history and files it never read, to xAI-controlled Google Cloud Storage despite the model-training opt-out being disabled. xAI appears to have shut the behavior off server-side, but users who ran the tool should rotate any credentials that may have been in read files, tracked files, or Git history.

  • A researcher testing Grok Build version 0.2.93 found that the CLI uploaded entire tracked Git repositories, including full commit history, to an xAI-controlled Google Cloud Storage bucket rather than only files needed for a coding task.
  • In one test on a 12 GB repository, traffic to the model endpoint was about 192 KB while the storage channel sent 5.10 GiB to /v1/storage in 73 chunks of about 75 MB each.
  • The researcher recovered a file named src/_probe/never_read_canary.txt from the captured Git bundle even though the agent had been explicitly told not to open it, and the result was replicated on a second unrelated repository.
  • Turning off the “Improve the model” setting did not stop the repository uploads, while the server response still returned trace_upload_enabled: true.
  • On July 13, the same 0.2.93 client stopped making storage requests after server-side settings changed to disable_codebase_upload: true and trace_upload_enabled: false, but xAI had not confirmed whether the change applied to every account or was permanent.

11 Malicious NuGet Tools Pose as Game Cheats to Drop a Windows Host-Surveillance Payload — Should Read

Socket researchers found 11 malicious NuGet .NET tools posing as game cheats that download and run a Windows payload called pepesoft.exe from GitHub or Hugging Face. The payload fingerprints hosts, reports licensing and telemetry to Google Sheets, supports remote bans, and in some builds can capture and send screenshots via Telegram.

  • Socket’s Threat Research Team analyzed 11 malicious NuGet packages published as .NET command-line tools that masquerade as game utilities, bots, and panels.
  • Each package acts as a first-stage downloader that fetches and executes a Windows payload named pepesoft.exe from GitHub Releases and Hugging Face paths under the username pepegit666.
  • The downloader stage resolves GitHub download hosts through Google DNS-over-HTTPS instead of the system resolver, and 10 of the 11 downloaders request elevation to resync the Windows system clock before fetching the payload.
  • The recovered pepesoft.exe payloads use downloader-supplied AWS-style key material to retrieve remote configuration, authenticate to Google Sheets, bind activations to hardware, and honor a remote hardware ID or UUID ban-list.
  • The direct-bytecode Albion, Calculator, and Throne payloads include Telegram bot commands that can capture and send screenshots back to the configured chat.

US unseals indictment against alleged operators of Russian bulletproof hosting service — Should Read

The U.S. unsealed charges against three Russians accused of running Media Land and ML Cloud, bulletproof hosting services allegedly used by ransomware gangs and cybercrime markets tied to $62 million in victim losses. Authorities also offered up to $10 million for information, particularly on any foreign government links.

  • Federal prosecutors unsealed an indictment against three Russians associated with Media Land and ML Cloud, a bulletproof hosting provider and sister company sanctioned by the U.S., U.K. and Australia in November.
  • Aleksandr Volosovik, Yulia Pankova and Kirill Zatolokin face charges including conspiracy to commit and aid and abet computer fraud, conspiracy to commit wire fraud, wire fraud, and conspiracy to commit money laundering.
  • The indictment cites 44 unnamed victims who suffered $62 million in losses from cybercriminal groups allegedly aided by Media Land and ML Cloud.
  • Authorities said ransomware groups including Lockbit, BlackSuit and Play, as well as stolen credit card marketplaces such as Briansclub and Bidencash, used Media Land infrastructure.
  • The U.S. State Department offered a reward of up to $10 million for information in the case, with an emphasis on information about foreign government links to Media Land and ML Cloud activities.

Researchers Say Claude for Chrome Flaw Lets Rogue Extensions Trigger Gmail Reads — Should Read

Researchers say Claude for Chrome still lets another extension that can script claude.ai forge a click to launch allowlisted tasks that may read Gmail, Google Docs, or Calendar data. Users are most at risk if “Act without asking” is enabled, because the task can run without an approval prompt, and no patch was available as of July 14.

  • Manifold Security says Claude for Chrome v1.0.80 still lets any other browser extension that can run a script on claude.ai trigger fixed Claude tasks aimed at Gmail, Google Docs, and Calendar.
  • The issue relies on a content script that accepts a synthetic click on a specific claude.ai element without checking whether the click came from a real user.
  • In the default mode, the forged task still shows an approval box that the user must click, but with “Act without asking” enabled the task runs without a prompt.
  • A second issue lets Claude’s side panel start in a mode that skips permission checks when its URL includes “skipPermissions=true,” though the article says this is not remotely reachable today.
  • Manifold reported the issues to Anthropic on May 21 against v1.0.72, and The Hacker News confirmed the same mechanisms remained in v1.0.80 as of July 14.

Study of 85 Crypto Wallet Extensions Finds Address Leaks and Cross-Site Tracking Risks — Should Read

KU Leuven researchers found that many popular browser-based crypto wallets leak wallet addresses or expose installed-wallet fingerprints, enabling address linking and cross-site tracking even without a hack. Users can reduce stale permissions manually, but the core privacy risks require wallet vendors and Web3 standards to change how wallets interact with sites and embedded frames.

  • KU Leuven researchers tested 85 popular crypto wallet browser extensions with about 35 million Chrome Web Store users and found privacy weaknesses that can link and track wallet users.
  • Seventeen wallets exposed links between a user’s separate addresses, with 13 bundling multiple addresses into one request and four sending separate requests within milliseconds of each other.
  • The researchers found that 36 of the 85 wallets announce themselves to any page they load, creating an installed-wallet fingerprint even if the user never connects a wallet or blocks cookies.
  • In 22 of those 36 wallets, a site could still read a user’s address after asking the wallet to revoke access, and that access survived clearing cookies and restarting the browser.
  • Of the same 36 wallets, 23 would provide a user’s address from inside an embedded frame, enabling a shared tracker to connect a wallet address with a name or email on another site if the embedded app is already authorized and allows embedding.

148 npm Packages Disguised as Student Proxies Turned Browsers Into a DDoS Botnet — Should Read

JFrog found 148 npm packages posing as student web proxies that secretly turned visitors’ browsers into a DDoS botnet, using HTTP floods and WebSocket attacks while avoiding traditional install-time detection. Although many packages were removed, the operators can potentially re-enable the capability through a remote loader without updating the npm packages.

  • JFrog reported that 148 npm packages disguised as student web proxies turned visitors’ browsers into a distributed denial-of-service botnet for roughly two weeks in May.
  • The packages carried proxy apps branded as Lucide and presented as tutoring landing pages, while secretly loading a remote code loader and a WebSocket flood generator before the React interface rendered.
  • An archived payload showed a remote script sending no-cors POST requests every 500 milliseconds to cdn.caan.edu, which JFrog identified as the public domain of a nursing school in Matteson, Illinois.
  • The WebSocket module fetched a configuration file and opened connections to a Wisp endpoint on lunaron[.]top, repeatedly sending valid Wisp CONNECT and CLOSE frames to stress the remote Wisp server.
  • JFrog said the DDoS modules were removed on May 31 as reporting began, but the current build still uses obfuscation, third-party scripts from attacker domains, and a loader pointing at a mutable branch that could be changed without a package update.

Burnt by Burgers: Highlighting Void Blizzard’s Russian State Links — Should Read

Ctrl-Alt-Intel found OSINT evidence linking alleged Void Blizzard member Denis Obrezko to Russia’s EMERCOM Information and Analytical Center, including work-associated phone data and repeated 2021 deliveries to EMERCOM facilities. The findings add state-institution context to US allegations that Obrezko worked with FSB-linked Yutek-NN on Russian cyberespionage operations.

  • Russian citizen Denis Obrezko was arrested in Thailand at the FBI’s request, extradited to the United States, and indicted for alleged participation in the Russian state-aligned threat group Void Blizzard, also known as Laundry Bear.
  • US filings allege that Obrezko worked in an unknown capacity for the FSB between approximately 2012 and 2017 and later served as deputy director of the Russian technology company Yutek-NN from at least 2024.
  • Ctrl-Alt-Intel identified breached-data evidence linking FBI-attributed Obrezko identifiers to an IAC EMERCOM-associated work number and repeated weekday food deliveries to EMERCOM facilities in Moscow during 2021.
  • Public records show that Yutek-NN holds an FSB-issued license covering surveillance-adjacent technology, though Ctrl-Alt-Intel states this does not independently prove the company conducted espionage.
  • Public Habr Career data showed three declared career transitions between Yutek-NN and IAC EMERCOM, suggesting personnel links between the organizations.

Spanish Police take down €140 million cyber fraud ring, arrest four — Should Read

Spanish police dismantled an international cyber fraud and money-laundering ring accused of moving about €140 million from investment scams and business email compromise attacks. Four suspects were arrested across Spain, Portugal, and Panama, with €3 million frozen for victims.

  • Spanish Police dismantled a cybercrime and money-laundering organization that made €140 million from investment fraud and business email compromise attacks.
  • Four people were arrested in Spain, Portugal, and Panama as part of an international operation supported by Interpol and Europol.
  • Police said the scheme used at least 800 bank accounts, 120 business accounts, and 67 external accomplices acting as money mules.
  • Investigators confirmed that €94 million was channeled through the network and linked another €61 million to the group’s 2024 business email compromise operations.
  • Authorities seized 15 computers and more than 170 smartphones and immediately froze €3 million in crime proceeds for victims.

LabubaRAT Masquerades as NVIDIA Software to Control Windows Hosts — Should Read

Researchers uncovered LabubaRAT, a Rust-based remote access trojan that disguises itself as NVIDIA software while giving attackers broad control over Windows hosts. Its runtime configuration and multiple C2 channels, including HTTPS, WebView2, and DNS tunneling, suggest it is built for reuse across campaigns and may be offered as malware-as-a-service.

  • Blackpoint Cyber researchers identified LabubaRAT, a previously undocumented Rust-based remote access trojan that masquerades as NVIDIA software to blend into target environments.
  • LabubaRAT supports multiple communication methods, including HTTPS, WebView2, and DNS tunneling, which can help attackers maintain access if one pathway is detected and closed off.
  • The attack chain begins with an executable named nvidia-sysruntime.exe, which impersonates NVIDIA's container runtime toolkit and accepts command-and-control configuration through command-line arguments.
  • LabubaRAT stores its configuration in a local SQLite database and profiles the host by checking for web browsers, security products, hostname, RAM size, CPU model, and Windows User Account Control state.
  • The malware can execute commands, run PowerShell and JavaScript, capture screenshots, upload and download files, handle archives, and provide SOCKS5 proxy support.

LastPass, Bitwarden users targeted with fake security alerts — Should Read

LastPass and Bitwarden users are being targeted by phishing emails posing as security policy updates that lead to fake DocuSign-style sites and prompt file downloads. LastPass says its systems were not compromised and urges users not to enter credentials, report suspicious messages, and change master passwords if they interacted with the sites.

  • LastPass warned users about an ongoing phishing campaign that uses fake security notices to direct recipients to fraudulent websites.
  • The phishing emails are sent from hello@lastpassnewsletter.com and claim LastPass has updated service policies, including enhanced SaaS monitoring, master password reset options for administrators, and admin console improvements.
  • Clicking the email’s “Review & Access Terms” button takes users to a fake DocuSign website on lastpasscompliance[.]com, which Microsoft Defender for Office 365 and Cloudflare flagged as malicious.
  • BleepingComputer found that Bitwarden users are targeted by similar emails sent from hello@bitwardennewsletter.com and redirected to bitwardencompliance[.]com.
  • LastPass said its systems were not compromised, the phishing emails did not originate from its infrastructure, and users who entered credentials on phishing sites should change their master passwords immediately from a trusted device.

Microsoft Entra ID gets passkeys default authentication starting September — Should Read

Microsoft Entra ID will make passkeys the default authentication method starting September 2026, automatically prompting SMS and voice MFA users to register passkeys. Microsoft will retire native SMS and voice authentication on February 1, 2027, so organizations must move users to phishing-resistant methods to avoid sign-in disruptions.

  • Microsoft announced that passkeys will become the default authentication method for the Entra ID enterprise identity service starting in September 2026.
  • Entra ID users currently using phone-based SMS and voice authentication will be automatically enabled for passkeys and prompted to register a passkey the next time they perform multifactor authentication.
  • Microsoft will retire Microsoft-provided telecom delivery for SMS and voice authentication on February 1, 2027, and will no longer offer SMS and voice as a native Microsoft Entra capability.
  • Organizations are advised to ensure all users adopt a phishing-resistant authentication method before February 1, 2027, to avoid sign-in disruptions.
  • Microsoft said making passkeys the default authentication experience reduces reliance on phishable authentication methods and strengthens protection against credential theft and phishing.

A Fake Malwarebytes Renewal, Signed by Google — Should Read

A fake Malwarebytes renewal invoice was sent via a legitimate Google Calendar invite from a newly registered Google Workspace domain, using phone numbers instead of malicious links or files to push a vishing scam. Because Google signed the message and all links were legitimate, detection depended on behavioral signals like the unknown organizer domain, brand mismatch, callback numbers, and user reporting.

  • An attacker registered betskl[.]com, created a Google Workspace account on it, and used Google Calendar to send a fake Malwarebytes Security Operations renewal invoice to a senior executive at a hospitality company.
  • The calendar invite claimed a $598.75 four-year Malwarebytes Premium Family Plan charge and provided two phone numbers for the recipient to call to dispute the supposed unauthorized charge.
  • The message contained no malicious links or code-bearing attachment, because its links resolved to calendar.google.com and the invite.ics attachment was a plain Google-generated iCalendar file.
  • DKIM and composite authentication passed because Google sent and signed the message, while the organizer address was an unrelated newly registered domain with no SPF or DMARC records.
  • The executive reported the message as an unknown sender, Themis identified it as suspicious vishing targeting a VIP recipient, and the message was quarantined and permanently deleted.

Finland issues wanted notice for hacker behind massive psychotherapy data breach — May Read

Finnish police have issued a wanted notice for convicted Vastaamo hacker Aleksanteri Kivimäki after the Supreme Court declined to hear his appeal, making his nearly seven-year sentence final. Authorities are seeking to return him to prison for the massive psychotherapy data breach and extortion of thousands of patients.

  • Finnish police issued a wanted notice for convicted hacker Aleksanteri Kivimäki after Finland’s Supreme Court refused to hear his appeal.
  • The Supreme Court’s decision leaves in place a February Court of Appeal ruling sentencing Kivimäki to nearly seven years in prison for hacking psychotherapy provider Vastaamo and extorting both the company and its patients.
  • Eastern Uusimaa Police said officers have been instructed to arrest Kivimäki if he is located and transfer him to Vantaa Prison to serve the rest of his sentence.
  • Kivimäki has denied carrying out the attack and argued that prosecutors relied largely on circumstantial evidence and disputed digital and cryptocurrency evidence.
  • The Vastaamo breach exposed information on about 33,000 patients, and more than 24,000 people reported receiving extortion demands.

J-Space: The Logs AI Security Has Never Had — May Read

Anthropic’s J-space research suggests AI agents may have an internal “intent” signal that can reveal deception, prompt injection awareness, or sabotage before visible actions occur. The article argues frontier labs should expose this telemetry to enterprise security teams so it can become a new layer of AI detection and response.

  • Anthropic’s interpretability research found a small internal structure in Claude called the J-space that carries deliberate multi-step reasoning and can reveal concepts in the model’s mind before they appear in output.
  • The J-lens technique reads the J-space by mapping internal activity patterns to words the model is more likely to say later, producing a list of concepts present during a model run.
  • Anthropic observed J-space signals such as “ERROR,” “injection,” “fake,” “manipulation,” “secretly,” “deliberately,” and “fraud” in scenarios involving bugs, prompt injections, staged blackmail tests, score manipulation, and sabotage-trained models.
  • The article argues that J-space telemetry would add a third layer of AI agent monitoring beyond what an agent says and does, enabling detection teams to correlate internal signals with tool actions and agent workflows.
  • The article calls on Anthropic and other frontier labs to expose workspace telemetry to enterprise customers because organizations running AI agents currently receive no J-space feed, API, or logs.

AI Security Report 2026 — May Read

Check Point Research’s AI Security Report 2026 warns that AI has moved from helping attackers to actively operating intrusions, generating malware, scaling phishing/vishing, and enabling convincing identity fraud. It also highlights growing risks from prompt injection and enterprise data leakage as organizations rapidly adopt GenAI tools.

  • Check Point Research’s Annual AI Security Report 2026 says AI has moved from being an assistant that helps attackers prepare to an operator that performs hands-on work inside live intrusions.
  • The report says AI now builds deployment-ready malware and attack suites, including VoidLink, an 88,000-line command-and-control offensive framework produced in under a week using an AI environment.
  • The report says attackers commonly prefer jailbroken mainstream commercial models and increasingly abuse agentic architecture by planting configuration files that agents load and trust across sessions.
  • The report says virtual identity is no longer a reliable trust anchor because voice, face, documents, and live video are now cheap to forge convincingly and are widely used in attacks.
  • The report says enterprise data leakage through GenAI is a persistent and growing risk, with high-risk prompts doubling from 2% to 4% during the last year.

The serpent’s tongue: Luring the Python out of its den — Optional

Python packages can execute malicious code during installation or later through abused packaging features like setup hooks, .pth files, sitecustomize, entry points, and import-time payloads, making supply-chain attacks dangerous even without directly running the package. Defenders should reduce risk with dependency auditing, pinned versions and hashes, isolated build environments, cooldown windows, SBOMs, and trusted publishing.

  • Python’s readable syntax, broad adoption, and extensive third-party library ecosystem make it an attractive target for threat actors seeking to compromise developer devices and infrastructure.
  • Malicious Python packages can execute payloads during installation through source distribution build mechanisms such as setup.py, meaning victims do not necessarily need to import or directly run the package code.
  • Python package features such as .pth files, sitecustomize.py, usercustomize.py, PYTHONPATH manipulation, __init__.py, __main__.py, entry points, and package directory name collisions can be abused for transient, persistent, or conditional payload execution.
  • The article groups malicious Python package techniques into build hook abuses and package content abuses, and evaluates them by operating system support, persistence, supported build methods, and distribution compatibility.
  • Recommended defenses include using pip-audit and Yara or AST scanning, pinning dependency versions with lock files and cryptographic hashes, using isolated build environments and dependency cooldowns, generating SBOMs, and adopting PyPI Trusted Publishing with OIDC.

Frontier AI in the Health Sector: Managing Supply Chain and Vendor Risk — Optional

Health-ISAC warns that frontier AI can accelerate vulnerability discovery so quickly that healthcare organizations must move from weeks-long patch cycles to remediation in days or hours. The paper urges providers to update vendor contracts, improve third-party visibility, and prepare contingency plans for AI-enabled supply chain risk.

  • Frontier AI models, including new large language models, can find vulnerabilities at an unprecedented pace, putting health sector systems and data at risk.
  • Health sector organizations need to prioritize vulnerability management, patching, and verification of patches on timelines measured in days or hours rather than weeks.
  • The paper says third-party supplier relationships are more complicated because existing contracts and service-level agreements may need to change as the threat model changes.
  • Health-ISAC member survey data indicates that roughly 80% of members are increasing budgets for AI-powered security solutions or proactively scanning their networks for weaknesses.
  • The paper recommends maintaining a comprehensive inventory of third-party software, developing contingency strategies, mapping external digital assets, adopting zero-trust principles, and maintaining transparent communication with supply chain partners.

The State of Enterprise Cyber Crisis Readiness (report) — Optional

A global survey of 1,000 organizations found that despite having and testing cyber incident response plans, most still struggle with major response blockers and cross-team coordination gaps. The key takeaway is that cyber crisis readiness depends less on more staffing and more on integrated, organization-wide communication and exercises.

  • The report is based on a global study of 1,000 organizations across the United States, United Kingdom, Europe, and the Asia-Pacific region.
  • The study found a disconnect between organizations’ perceived cyber crisis readiness and their actual performance during cyber incidents.
  • Ninety percent of organizations reported serious blockers to effective cyber response.
  • Less than 50% of organizations conduct tabletop exercises that include all teams commonly involved in an actual crisis.
  • Seventy-one percent of organizations experienced at least one high-impact cyber incident that disrupted critical business functions in the past year, and 36% suffered multiple damaging incidents.

AI Agents Are Creating a New Class of Employee Risk — Optional

AI agents are becoming autonomous “digital employees” with access to sensitive enterprise data, creating new risks when they act too quickly or without sufficient context. Organizations need data-centric controls that evaluate actions and intent in real time, not just static access permissions.

  • AI agents are creating a new digital workforce that increases the number of non-human identities accessing sensitive data.
  • The article cites PocketOS as an example where Cursor deleted the business, including its database and backups, after finding a discrepancy during a routine task.
  • AI agents can act autonomously on enterprise data, which increases the speed of risk and changes how risk is created.
  • The article says model safeguards alone are not enough because AI agents do not inherently understand risk or policy.
  • Organizations need a data-centric security layer that connects data sensitivity, permissions, identity, and activity to decide whether an action should be allowed.

Varonis Atlas Extends Coverage Across the Claude Enterprise Suite — From Claude Cowork to Claude Code — Optional

Varonis announced expanded Atlas support across Anthropic’s Claude enterprise suite, adding coverage for Claude Code and Claude Cowork alongside existing Claude Enterprise and Platform integrations. The key takeaway is that Atlas now aims to provide unified security monitoring, runtime guardrails, and incident visibility across Claude’s assistant, developer, and agentic file-access surfaces.

  • Varonis Atlas now secures the entire Claude enterprise suite, extending existing support for Claude Enterprise and Claude Platform to Claude Code and Claude Cowork.
  • The article says Atlas covers Anthropic assistant products, developer tools, and infrastructure used to build and deploy Claude agents, including Microsoft Foundry, AWS Bedrock, and Claude Platform.
  • For Claude Code, Atlas provides runtime guardrails, AI detection and response, posture management, and activity monitoring across prompts, LLM calls, tool calls, MCP interactions, command execution, and agent actions.
  • For Claude Cowork, Atlas supports a dedicated runtime integration that sends Cowork activity to Atlas so policies can block, modify, alert on, or log activity as it happens.
  • The article states that comprehensive Claude coverage is needed because Anthropic agents can now take actions such as writing local files, running terminal commands, and editing code.

AI Productivity Tools: The Adoption Journey So Far — Optional

AI productivity tools can deliver major gains for security teams, but the real challenge is learning how to use the right tool for the right task while continuously improving prompts, workflows, and team knowledge sharing. The author argues there is no fixed benchmark for being “productive enough”; the sustainable goal is simply to get better than yesterday.

  • The author says eight months of using AI productivity tools has made him measurably more productive, sometimes by 3x to 5x, but he still finds it difficult to know what level of productivity is enough.
  • The author uses different AI tools for different tasks, including ChatGPT for everyday brainstorming and questions, Claude for deeper research and planning, Claude Code and Cursor for coding, and NotebookLM for learning and organizing research.
  • The author built a full internal application for Mitiga’s research team in about five hours with Claude, including conference tracking, submission review, dashboards, Slack notifications, SSO, deployment, and security audits.
  • The author says AI changed his work style by making it easier to run several workstreams in parallel because he can refocus on the current status and next task instead of holding the entire problem in his head.
  • The author argues that poor AI results are usually caused by vague prompts, failure to break work into smaller parts, or not knowing the desired outcome clearly enough.

You Don't Have to Run an Exploit to Know If You're Vulnerable — Optional

As CVEs and AI-assisted exploitation outpace patching, the article argues that defenders should prioritize validating whether exploit chains would actually succeed in their environment rather than relying only on live exploits or patch queues. It promotes Picus’s approach of safely testing attack behaviors and control effectiveness to identify which vulnerabilities are truly exploitable.

  • The article says the first half of 2026 produced more CVEs than any full year before 2024, with new flaws arriving at about one every 7.4 minutes.
  • The article states that AI has reduced the median time-to-exploit for 2026 to well under a day, down from weeks a few years earlier.
  • The article argues that live exploit testing is limited because it can only be used where it is safe and where a usable exploit exists, which it says covers only 10 to 15% of most enterprises’ attack surface.
  • The article says Picus can validate exploitability by mapping a vulnerability to the steps an attacker would need and testing whether each step is blocked by deployed defenses.
  • The article uses Nightmare-Eclipse Windows zero-days, including BlueHammer, RedSun, and UnDefend, as an example of proving an attack chain without running the actual malware against a domain controller.

How Pentera Turns AI Security Workflows into Validation Engines — Optional

Pentera is positioning its MCP Server as a way to feed validated attack-path evidence into AI security workflows, so teams can prioritize and remediate risks proven to be exploitable rather than relying on scanner scores or fragmented signals. The key takeaway is that AI-driven security decisions become more useful when grounded in validation data that shows what attackers can actually exploit in the environment.

  • The article argues that AI security workflows based only on fragmented signals such as scanner output, severity scores, threat intelligence, configuration findings, and exposure data cannot prove whether findings form real attack paths.
  • Pentera’s AI-powered security validation platform safely emulates real-world attack techniques against production environments to determine which exposures can actually be leveraged by an attacker.
  • Pentera generates validated attack paths with evidence including the technique used, systems reached, credentials obtained, privileges gained, assets at risk, and objective achieved.
  • Pentera introduced an MCP Server that makes Pentera validation data available directly to MCP-compatible AI assistants through existing AI-based tools and natural-language workflows.
  • Pentera’s MCP Server is designed for controlled enterprise deployments by running locally as a Docker container, using STDIO communication, opening no inbound ports, inheriting existing Pentera RBAC permissions, and logging interactions for auditability.

10 Black Hat NOCs and Counting: Corelight Sees It All | Corelight — Optional

Corelight highlights its long-running role supporting the Black Hat network operations center, emphasizing how its network visibility helps monitor and defend one of the world’s most challenging conference networks.

  • The article is titled “10 Black Hat NOCs and Counting: Corelight Sees It All.”
  • The article identifies Corelight as the organization associated with the content.
  • The article references Black Hat NOCs and the number 10 in connection with Corelight.

Human Risk Management 90-Day Playbook — Optional

Living Security’s 90-Day Human Risk Management Playbook outlines how healthcare organizations can move beyond generic compliance training to a data-driven program that identifies high-risk users and delivers targeted microlearning. The key takeaway is that focusing on the riskiest employees can produce measurable reductions in phishing-related behavior within one quarter.

  • The article presents the Human Risk Management 90-Day Playbook from Living Security, a Health-ISAC Community Champion.
  • The playbook provides a modular, outcome-oriented roadmap for transforming generic training into a data-driven engine for risk reduction.
  • The article says most awareness programs are stuck in a compliance loop and see only 12% of actual human risk.
  • The playbook aims to help organizations surface the riskiest 10% of their workforce and automate targeted microlearning.
  • The article cites potential measurable wins such as cutting repeat clickers by 40% and increasing report rates by 15% in one quarter.

Microsoft starts testing cleaner Windows Search without ads — Optional

Microsoft is testing a cleaner Windows Search for Windows 11 Insiders that prioritizes relevant local results over ads and promotional content. The update adds clearer result sources, controls for web and Microsoft Store suggestions, improved file/app search, and reliability fixes.

  • Microsoft is testing a cleaner and faster version of Windows Search that is intended to prioritize relevant results over ads and promotional content.
  • The Windows Search Box updates are available to Windows Insiders in the Experimental channel through a Controlled Feature Rollout that began rolling out on Monday.
  • Windows Search results now more clearly show whether they come from an app, Windows setting, file, web result, or Microsoft Store suggestion.
  • A new setting under Settings > Privacy & Security > Search lets users choose whether Microsoft Store and web suggestions appear alongside local results.
  • Microsoft says the updated search more reliably prioritizes local content, supports two-character file searches, improves cloud file visibility, better handles typos and partial words for app searches, and includes reliability fixes.

[Video] Where protection starts: Cisco Talos Intelligence Integrations — Optional

Cisco is promoting its Talos Intelligence Integrations, which apply Talos threat intelligence across Cisco security and enterprise products to help identify and block malicious activity. The article points readers to a new video explaining how these integrations work and who builds them.

  • Security teams are often asked to make decisions with incomplete information while attackers benefit from defenders not seeing the full picture.
  • The article says defenders now face attackers using AI to rewrite malicious commands, malware that changes its code on each installation, and models that search old vulnerable code and exposed interfaces for exploitation opportunities.
  • Cisco Talos Intelligence Integrations are presented as a way to help answer questions such as whether a newly registered domain is part of an attack, an outbound connection is normal, or user behavior is unusual.
  • Across Cisco security and enterprise technologies, Talos reputation and detection integrations continuously apply current threat intelligence to identify and block malicious activity.
  • The article introduces a video featuring Talos team members who explain how the Talos Intelligence Integrations work.

Introducing the Silent Push Partner Program — Optional

Silent Push has launched its Partner Portal and formal Channel Partner Program to support its 55+ global partners with sales, marketing, and enablement resources for taking its preemptive threat intelligence offering to market.

  • Silent Push is launching the Silent Push Partner Portal and officially announcing its Channel Partner Program.
  • Silent Push says it already has more than 55 partners globally, including distributors, MSSPs, systems integrators, and technology resellers.
  • The partner portal provides branded assets, product collateral, white papers, datasheets, co-sell resources, campaign assets, and a direct line to the Silent Push team.
  • Silent Push says its proprietary Indicators of Future Attack data gives security teams visibility into adversary infrastructure before it is weaponized.
  • Silent Push plans to roll out partner spotlights, onboard new regional partners, and add ongoing training and enablement content to the portal.
